claims.claim: Stonehenge's Altar Stone was traced to Scotland in 2024. Where exactly it came from is still unknown
claims.source_checked: api.crossref.org/works/10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1 (title, abstract, online 2024-08-14); Clarke 2024 full text via Firecrawl research index (pmcid:PMC11324516); api.crossref.org/works/10.1144/jgs2026-090 (ABSTRACT ONLY); api.crossref.org/works/10.1002/jqs.70080 (ABSTRACT ONLY)
claims.note: Clarke 2024 title 'A Scottish provenance for the Altar Stone of Stonehenge', online 14 Aug 2024; body: data 'indicate that the Altar Stone of Stonehenge has a provenance from the ORS in the Orcadian Basin of northeast Scotland'. Pirrie 2026 abstract: 'the exact provenance of the Altar Stone is as yet unknown'; Clarke 2026 abstract: 'its source location within this large basin remains unresolved'. Neither 2026 abstract says the stone is not from Scotland, so the title leaves no false belief (A4).

claims.claim: In 2024, Stonehenge's Altar Stone was traced to Scotland.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1: Crossref abstract and full text via the research index (pmcid:PMC11324516)
claims.note: Abstract: detrital ages 'reveal a remarkable similarity to the Old Red Sandstone of the Orcadian Basin in northeast Scotland'; body states a provenance from the Orcadian Basin ORS. Published online 14 August 2024. A viewer who swipes at second two hears only this hook over a photo of Stonehenge; it states what the 2024 paper found and nothing later contradicts it.

claims.claim: Exactly where it came from is still unknown.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1144/jgs2026-090 and doi:10.1002/jqs.70080: ABSTRACTS ONLY (Crossref; Lyell and Wiley full text behind a bot challenge, 403); doi:10.14324/AI.27.1.13 full text (PDF from journals.uclpress.co.uk/ai/article/3293/galley/18572/download/)
claims.note: Pirrie 2026 abstract: 'the exact provenance of the Altar Stone is as yet unknown' (nearly the script's words). Clarke 2026 abstract: 'its source location within this large basin remains unresolved'. 'Still' holds: Parker Pearson 2024: 'As yet, the actual outcrop from which the Altar Stone was extracted is unknown'; Clarke 2024 named a basin, not an outcrop.

claims.claim: The ages of tiny mineral grains inside it matched sandstone in the northeast.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1 full text via research index (pmcid:PMC11324516): 'Orcadian Basin ORS' section and Methods
claims.note: U-Pb/Lu-Hf ages of zircon, apatite and rutile grains 'typically 10–40 µm wide' (dated grains 'usually <30 µm in width'), so 'tiny' is fair. 'The detrital zircon age spectra from Orcadian Basin ORS provides the closest match'; KS test cannot separate them; apatite age components from Spittal (Caithness) and Cruaday (Orkney) 'match those from the Altar Stone'. Svalbard ORS zircon is also statistically indistinguishable, but the line claims a match, not a unique one, and the apatite comparison is with NE Scotland samples.

claims.note: Methods: 'Resistive heavy mineral bands are dominated by zircon, rutile, and apatite, with grains typically 10–40 µm wide.' The drawing is labelled as an illustration, not to scale (A6).

claims.claim: If so, how did six tonnes travel more than seven hundred kilometres?

claims.note: Clarke 2024 abstract: 'a 6 tonne shaped block, was sourced at least 750 km from its current location'; body: 'measuring 4.9 × 1.0 × 0.5 m ... weighing 6 t'; 'a Scottish provenance ... demands a transport distance of at least 750 km'. Clarke 2026: '6000 kg', 'some 700 km'. 'More than seven hundred' fits both. 'If so' keeps the distance conditional on a NE Scotland source, as the papers frame it.

claims.note: Clarke 2024 says only that geography 'would have permitted sea routes southward from the Orcadian Basin towards southern England' and names no route; Clarke 2026 abstract: 'mode of transport uncertain'. So 'route not known' is right and drawing both coasts is honest. Geometry: all 12 EAST and 16 WEST points are at sea, and all 11 + 15 segments have 0 coastline crossings and 0 land samples against coast.json; closest passes (Portland Bill, Mull of Oa, Mull of Kintyre, Land's End) are a few km offshore.

claims.claim: But no late Stone Age boat has been found in Britain,
claims.source_checked: doi:10.14324/AI.27.1.13 full text (UCL Press PDF), section 'How was the Altar Stone transported?'
claims.note: 'Although no boats are known from the Late Neolithic in Britain or Europe'; and 'The earliest known boats in Britain have been found ... at Ferriby. The earliest of these Early Bronze Age sewn-plank boats (Ferriby 3) dates to 2030–1780 cal bc'. So the claim holds whether 'late Stone Age' is read narrowly (Late Neolithic) or broadly (any Stone Age boat): the paper says the earliest known boats in Britain are Early Bronze Age.

claims.claim: NO BOAT FOUND / from the late Stone Age, in Britain

claims.claim: and another study doubts one could carry six tonnes.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.14324/AI.27.1.13 full text (UCL Press PDF)
claims.note: 'What we know of Early Bronze Age boats ... would suggest that they and their Late Neolithic precursors were unlikely to be sturdy enough to carry a 6-tonne stone in coastal waters.' 'Doubts' = 'unlikely'; 'one' = a boat of that period. 'Another study' is literally true (a different paper), though three of its six authors (Bevins, Ixer, Pearce) also wrote Clarke 2024; the script does not call it independent.

claims.claim: A glacier? A 2026 ice model says ice could have carried it part of the way, at most.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1002/jqs.70080 ABSTRACT ONLY (Crossref; online 2026-06-04; Wiley full text behind bot challenge, 403)
claims.note: Abstract: 'we combine sandstone provenance analysis with ice flow modelling'; from Caithness 'a localised south-eastward pathway directed towards Dogger Bank'; 'Glacial transport may have provided an intermediate stage in the stone's journey, but alone cannot account for the final emplacement on Salisbury Plain. Even under a glacially assisted scenario, substantial anthropogenic transport would have remained necessary.' 'Part of the way, at most' fits. Note the abstract adds a further problem the script omits (Dogger Bank was inundated before the stone likely arrived), which only weakens the glacier option; older sources (Clarke 2024, Parker Pearson 2024) reject glacial transport outright, so the script's wording is not stronger than any source.
